Now I have the real data — including the full **Opensignal December 2025 report** (90 days of measurements, Jul 1–Sep 28 2025, all four operators) [36], which contains the closest thing Sweden has to a published "stability" metric. Here's the deep version:

## 1. The honest framing: no public incident registry exists

PTS supervises outage handling and collects complaints, but publishes **no per-operator incident counts or uptime figures** — that's why every "stability comparison" you'll find online is inference. The deep sources that *do* exist are: (a) Opensignal's **Reliability Experience** metric — literally a measure of users' ability to connect and complete tasks without failure; (b) **Time on Network** — the share of time users have *no* connection at all; (c) regulatory supervision records; (d) structural analysis of the three physical networks.

## 2. The actual measured stability data (Opensignal Dec 2025) [36]

| Metric (closer = more stable) | **Tre** | **Telia** | **Telenor (Vimla's host)** | Tele2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Reliability Experience** (0–1000) | **943** 🏆 shared | 927 | **944** 🏆 | 912 |
| **Consistent Quality** (% of tests "good enough") | **84.3%** 🏆 | 82.8% | 84.0% 🏆 | 81.7% |
| **Time on Network** (connected %) | **99.7%** 🏆 | 99.3% | **99.7%** 🏆 | 99.6% |
| **Coverage Experience** (0–10) | **6.55 — last** | **7.67** 🏆 | 7.26 | 7.26 |
| **5G Coverage Experience** | **2.98 — far last** | 4.73 | **4.92** 🏆 | 4.92 |
| Time on 5G | 14.2% | 15.1% | **21.4%** 🏆 | 19.7% |

This changes the story in an important way. The **Reliability Experience** numbers — the closest published proxy for "how often do users hit failures" — show **Tre and Telenor statistically tied as the most reliable networks (943/944), with Telia slightly behind (927)** [36]. And Telia's Time-on-Network is the lowest (99.3% vs 99.7%) — meaning Telia users, measured across real usage including indoors, spend marginally more time with *zero* connection. The gap is small (~3 hours/month), but it's the *opposite* of the popular "Telia = most stable" assumption.

**The resolution of the paradox:** Tre's problem was never incident-frequency — where Tre covers, it's excellent (best Consistent Quality of all: 84.3%). Tre's problem is **footprint breadth**: its Coverage Experience (6.55) trails Telia's (7.67), and its 5G Coverage Experience (2.98) is **40% below** Telenor/Tele2's (4.92) — the direct, quantified fingerprint of missing n28 low-band 5G [36]. Telia's slight reliability deficit is the flip side of its strategy: pushing coverage deeper into harder places means more marginal connections per user. **Stability-as-outage-frequency: essentially equal. Stability-as-coverage-of-places-you-go: Telia ≫ Tre, Telenor in between.**

## 3. Structural resilience of the three hosts (deeper than awards)

- **Net4Mobility (Vimla's host):** founded April 2009 as a true joint venture — Telenor and Tele2 *co-own* the company that builds and operates one nationwide network across 700/800/900/1800/2100/2600/3500 MHz, covering 99.9% of population [9]. On 3 September 2025 they activated 5G across the *entire* network — 90% of Sweden's landmass — explicitly framed around **"rural reach and network resilience"** [36]. The structural risk we discussed stands: a shared-radio fault can hit both Telenor and Tele2 brands at once.
- **Telia:** own network, umlaut's #1 six years running, keeps **2G alive until end-2027 specifically to support IoT and emergency services** during the transition [36] — a deliberate resilience choice no other operator made.
- **Tre:** own network, SA first-mover, best Consistent Quality — but the 5G coverage gap (2.98) is structural, not fixable without new spectrum [36].
- **Post-3G transition risk (now resolved):** PTS warned that some devices would lose 112 access after 2G/3G shutdowns and **required Tele2, Telenor and Tre to guarantee emergency access — via a domestic roaming solution** [36]. Net4Mobility shut down both 2G and 3G on 1 Dec 2025 [36].

## 4. The regulatory/defense layer (the part rarely surfaced)

- **NIS2 has become Swedish law** (prop. 2025/26:28, July 2026) — stricter incident-prevention, risk-management and reporting duties for telecom as critical infrastructure; PTS runs active supervisory checks on spectrum-security conditions (including vendor-security requirements effective Jan 2025) [36].
- **Försvarsmakten's own submission to MSB** flags reserve power in core and mobile networks as *high-priority* — i.e., the known weak point in crisis scenarios is electricity, not operator competence; PTS has piloted mobile-site generator backup (Gotland) with results feeding mainland rollout.
- All four networks sit under the same critical-infrastructure regime — there is no "less regulated" operator among them.

## 5. Verdict — stability and incidents, deep-research edition

| Question | Answer with evidence |
|---|---|
| **Who has the most *incidents*?** | No public registry exists; all three hosts are critical infrastructure under NIS2/CER-grade rules. No recent major national outages found for any of them. Differences in *outage frequency* are not measurably significant. |
| **Who is most *reliable* as experienced?** | **Tre and Telenor statistically tied (943/944), Telia close behind (927)** [36] — Tre's reliability is excellent *within* its footprint. |
| **Where does Tre lose?** | Footprint, not stability: Coverage 6.55 vs Telia's 7.67; 5G coverage 2.98 vs 4.92 [36] — permanent dead zones, not incidents. |
| **Who has the most crisis-resilient architecture?** | Telia (2G to 2027 for emergencies, own everything, best populated-area coverage 7.67) and Net4Mobility (5G network-wide with explicit resilience focus, 99.9%) [9][36]; Tre strongest in cities, weakest footprint. |
| **Your household split (Fello/Telia + Vimla/Net4Mobility)?** | Validated by the data: the two hosts with the **top coverage scores and two different failure geometries** (isolated Telia grid vs shared Net4Mobility grid), both with 99%+ measured availability — and 112 now backed by a regulated domestic-roaming fallback after the legacy shutdown [36]. |

**The deep conclusion:** "stability" in Sweden isn't won by incident-avoidance — all three networks are engineered and regulated to near-parity there. The measurable differentiator is **Consistency × Coverage**: Tre maximizes consistency but minimizes footprint (your family's dead zones, now quantified as 2.98 on 5G coverage [36]); Telia maximizes footprint; Net4Mobility maximizes 5G coverage-per-population with a shared-grid blast radius. Your Fello+Vimla pairing sits on the two highest-coverage, highest-satisfaction, independently-failing networks — which is exactly what the crisis analysis recommended, now backed by measured reliability data rather than marketing.

Key Findings
------------

### Telenor users spend the most time connected to 5G

Time on 5G award (previously called 5G Availability) is now with Telenor, meaning that our Telenor users spend the highest proportion of time utilizing an active 5G connection, at 21.4% of the time.

### Telenor stays on top for overall download speeds, but Tele2 is now fastest on 5G

Telenor continues to win the Download Speed Experience award, with an average download speed of 84.7Mbps, and marginal lead over second-placed Tele2. On 5G, the winner of the 5G Download Speed award is now Tele2, which records 219Mbps, leading over Telenor by 7Mbps.

### Telia takes the 5G Upload Speed award

In this report, the winner of the 5G Upload Speed award is now Telia. Our Telia users see average 5G upload speeds of 20Mbps, giving Telia a lead of less than one Mbps over second-placed 3 (19.7Mbps). Tele2 comes third with 18.5Mbps, while Telenor places fourth on 17.5Mbps. However, 5G upload speeds have fallen across all operators compared with the previous report — 3 is down by 15Mbps, while Telia and Telenor are each down by 9Mbps and Tele2 is down by 8Mbps.

### Telia keeps the best overall coverage experience, while Telenor and Tele2 now lead for 5G coverage

Telia continues to keep hold of Coverage Experience, meaning our Telia users saw coverage most frequently across populated areas that they visited. Telia wins the award with 7.7 points on a 10-point scale, leading second-placed Telenor and Tele2 by less than one point. For 5G Coverage Experience, the winners are now Telenor and Tele2, sharing the award with identical scores of 4.9 points. They lead third-placed Telia (4.7 points) by less than one point.

Market Overview
---------------

Telenor is the most awarded operator this time around, winning 11 awards in total including the key experience metrics that qualify Telenor as Sweden’s Best Network, according to Opensignal’s Best Network methodology. Tele2 follows with eight awards (one outright — 5G Download Speed — and seven jointly), while 3 picks up seven awards, all jointly. Telia wins two awards outright (Coverage Experience and 5G Upload Speed).

Sweden’s mobile market is undergoing a major technology transition as operators move to retire legacy networks. The nationwide 3G shutdown is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2025, as communicated by [3](https://www.tre.se/varfor-tre/tackning/3g)
 and [Telia](https://www.telia.se/artiklar/innovation/sa-paverkas-du-nar-vi-avvecklar-3g-och-2g-naten)
. [Tele2 together with Telenor](https://www.tele2.com/sv/media/pressmeddelanden/2025/drygt-en-manad-kvar-tills-2g-och-3g-naten-slacks-vanta-inte-till-sista-stund/)
, through the Net4Mobility joint venture, have planned to switch off both 2G and 3G on 1 December 2025, while Telia intends to keep its 2G network operational until the end of 2027 to support IoT and emergency services. During the transition, the Swedish Post and Telecom Authority (PTS) has warned that some devices may lose access to the emergency number 112 after 2G/3G shutdowns — even if they appear to support 4G — and has [required](https://pts.se/en/news-and-press-releases/operators-must-ensure-access-to-112--certain-mobile-phones-will-be-blocked/)
 Tele2, Telenor and 3 to ensure continued emergency-call access, currently planned via a domestic roaming solution.

The retirement of 2G and 3G is central to operator strategy, freeing spectrum and operational resources to support rising data demand and further investment in 4G and 5G. In parallel with the shutdowns, Sweden’s 5G footprint continued to expand. On 3 September 2025, Tele2 and Telenor [announced](https://www.tele2.com/media/news/2025/tele2-and-telenor-now-activate-5g-across-the-entire-mobile-network-covering-90-of-swedens-landmass-and-99-9-of-the-population/)
 the activation of 5G across their entire mobile network, extending 5G coverage to match their 4G footprint — reported as reaching 99.9% of the population — with a focus on rural reach and network resilience. The rollout is delivered through [Net4Mobility](https://net4mobility.com/)
, their shared nationwide network.

Regulatory developments in 2025 have reinforced a focus on security and spectrum availability. In April, PTS began [supervisory checks](https://pts.se/nyheter-och-pressmeddelanden/pts-kontrollerar-att-mobiloperatorer-foljer-sakerhetsvillkor/)
 to assess compliance with security-related licence conditions in the 2.3GHz and 3.5GHz bands, including requirements linked to the use of equipment from suppliers such as Huawei and ZTE, which came into force on 1 January 2025. Later in the year, PTS also [concluded an auction](https://pts.se/en/news-and-press-releases/the-auction-in-the-1800-mhz-band-has-closed/)
 in the 1800MHz band, awarding licences to Net4Mobility and Telia to support future 4G and 5G capacity and coverage.

In this report we examine the mobile network experience of the four main mobile network operators in Sweden — 3, Tele2, Telenor and Telia — over a period of 90 days starting on July 1, 2025, and ending on September 28, 2025, to see how they fared.

### **Definitions**

Opensignal’s Video Experience quantifies the quality of video streamed to mobile devices by measuring real-world video streams over an operator's networks. The metric is based on an International Telecommunication Union (ITU) approach, built upon detailed studies which have derived a relationship between technical parameters, including picture quality, video loading time and stall rate, with the perceived video experience as reported by real people. To calculate video experience, we are directly measuring video streams from end-user devices and using this ITU approach to quantify the overall video experience for each operator on a scale from 0 to 100. The videos tested include a mixture of resolutions — including Full HD (FHD) and 4K / Ultra HD (UHD) — and are streamed directly from the world’s largest video content providers.

In addition to Video Experience, we report on the following metrics related to video experience:

*   5G Video Experience: The average Video Experience of Opensignal users when they were connected to an operator’s 5G network.
*   Video Experience – 5G Users: The average Video Experience of Opensignal users with a 5G device and a 5G subscription across an operator's networks. It factors in 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G video experience along with the availability of each technology.
*   4G Video Experience: The average Video Experience of Opensignal users on an operator's 4G network.
*   3G Video Experience: The average Video Experience of Opensignal users on an operator’s 3G network.

[Learn more](https://insights.opensignal.com/our-approach)

### **Definitions**

Opensignal’s Games Experience measures how mobile users experience real-time multiplayer mobile gaming on an operator’s network. Measured on a scale of 0-100, it analyzes how our users’ multiplayer mobile gaming experience is affected by mobile network conditions including latency, packet loss and jitter.

Games Experience quantifies the experience when playing real-time multiplayer mobile games on mobile devices connected to servers located around the world. The approach is built on several years of research quantifying the relationship between technical network parameters and the gaming experience as reported by real mobile users. These parameters include latency (round trip time), jitter (variability of latency) and packet loss (the proportion of data packets that never reach their destination). Additionally, it considers multiple genres of multiplayer mobile games to measure the average sensitivity to network conditions. The games tested include some of the most popular real-time multiplayer mobile games (such as Fortnite, Pro Evolution Soccer and Arena of Valor) played around the world.

Calculating Games Experience starts with measuring the end-to-end experience from users’ devices to internet end-points that host real games. The score is then measured on a scale from 0 to 100.

In addition to Games Experience, we report on the following metrics related to games experience:

*   5G Games Experience: The average Games Experience of Opensignal users when they were connected to an operator’s 5G network.
*   Games Experience – 5G Users: The average Games Experience of Opensignal users with a 5G device and a 5G subscription across an operator's networks. It factors in 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G games experience along with the availability of each technology.
*   4G Games Experience: The average Games Experience of Opensignal users on an operator's 4G network.
*   3G Games Experience: The average Games Experience of Opensignal users on an operator's 3G (e.g. UMTS/HSPA or CDMA 1X EV-DO) network.

[Learn more](https://insights.opensignal.com/our-approach)

### **Definitions**

Measured in Mbps, Download Speed Experience represents the typical everyday speeds a user experiences across an operator’s mobile data networks.

In addition to Download Speed Experience, we report on the following metrics related to download speeds:

*   5G Download Speed: The average download speed observed by Opensignal users with active 5G connections.
*   Download Speed Experience – 5G Users: The average download speeds experienced by Opensignal users with a 5G device and a 5G subscription across an operator’s networks. It factors in 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G download speeds along with the availability of each technology.
*   4G Download Speed: The average downlink speed observed by Opensignal users when they were connected to 4G.
*   3G Download Speed: The average downlink speed observed by Opensignal users when they were connected to 3G (e.g. UMTS/HSPA or CDMA 1X EV-DO).

[Learn more](https://insights.opensignal.com/our-approach)

### **Definitions**

Upload Speed Experience measures the average upload speeds for each operator observed by our users across their mobile data networks. Typically upload speeds are slower than download speeds, as current mobile broadband technologies focus resources on providing the best possible download speed for users consuming content on their devices. As mobile internet trends move away from downloading content to creating content and supporting real-time communications services, upload speeds are becoming more vital and new technologies are emerging that boost upstream capacity.

In addition to Upload Speed Experience, we report on five supporting metrics related to upload speeds:

*   5G Upload Speed: The average upload speed observed by Opensignal users with active 5G connections.
*   Upload Speed Experience – 5G Users: The average upload speeds experienced by Opensignal users with a 5G device and a 5G subscription across an operator’s networks. It factors in 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G upload speeds along with the availability of each technology.
*   4G Upload Speed: The average uplink speed observed by Opensignal users when they were connected to 4G.
*   3G Upload Speed: The average uplink speed observed by Opensignal users when they were connected to 3G (e.g. UMTS/HSPA or CDMA 1X EV-DO).

Now I have the real data — including the full **Opensignal December 2025 report** (90 days of measurements, Jul 1–Sep 28 2025, all four operators) [36], which contains the closest thing Sweden has to a published "stability" metric. Here's the deep version:

## 1. The honest framing: no public incident registry exists

PTS supervises outage handling and collects complaints, but publishes **no per-operator incident counts or uptime figures** — that's why every "stability comparison" you'll find online is inference. The deep sources that *do* exist are: (a) Opensignal's **Reliability Experience** metric — literally a measure of users' ability to connect and complete tasks without failure; (b) **Time on Network** — the share of time users have *no* connection at all; (c) regulatory supervision records; (d) structural analysis of the three physical networks.

## 2. The actual measured stability data (Opensignal Dec 2025) [36]

| Metric (closer = more stable) | **Tre** | **Telia** | **Telenor (Vimla's host)** | Tele2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Reliability Experience** (0–1000) | **943** 🏆 shared | 927 | **944** 🏆 | 912 |
| **Consistent Quality** (% of tests "good enough") | **84.3%** 🏆 | 82.8% | 84.0% 🏆 | 81.7% |
| **Time on Network** (connected %) | **99.7%** 🏆 | 99.3% | **99.7%** 🏆 | 99.6% |
| **Coverage Experience** (0–10) | **6.55 — last** | **7.67** 🏆 | 7.26 | 7.26 |
| **5G Coverage Experience** | **2.98 — far last** | 4.73 | **4.92** 🏆 | 4.92 |
| Time on 5G | 14.2% | 15.1% | **21.4%** 🏆 | 19.7% |

This changes the story in an important way. The **Reliability Experience** numbers — the closest published proxy for "how often do users hit failures" — show **Tre and Telenor statistically tied as the most reliable networks (943/944), with Telia slightly behind (927)** [36]. And Telia's Time-on-Network is the lowest (99.3% vs 99.7%) — meaning Telia users, measured across real usage including indoors, spend marginally more time with *zero* connection. The gap is small (~3 hours/month), but it's the *opposite* of the popular "Telia = most stable" assumption.

**The resolution of the paradox:** Tre's problem was never incident-frequency — where Tre covers, it's excellent (best Consistent Quality of all: 84.3%). Tre's problem is **footprint breadth**: its Coverage Experience (6.55) trails Telia's (7.67), and its 5G Coverage Experience (2.98) is **40% below** Telenor/Tele2's (4.92) — the direct, quantified fingerprint of missing n28 low-band 5G [36]. Telia's slight reliability deficit is the flip side of its strategy: pushing coverage deeper into harder places means more marginal connections per user. **Stability-as-outage-frequency: essentially equal. Stability-as-coverage-of-places-you-go: Telia ≫ Tre, Telenor in between.**

## 3. Structural resilience of the three hosts (deeper than awards)

- **Net4Mobility (Vimla's host):** founded April 2009 as a true joint venture — Telenor and Tele2 *co-own* the company that builds and operates one nationwide network across 700/800/900/1800/2100/2600/3500 MHz, covering 99.9% of population [9]. On 3 September 2025 they activated 5G across the *entire* network — 90% of Sweden's landmass — explicitly framed around **"rural reach and network resilience"** [36]. The structural risk we discussed stands: a shared-radio fault can hit both Telenor and Tele2 brands at once.
- **Telia:** own network, umlaut's #1 six years running, keeps **2G alive until end-2027 specifically to support IoT and emergency services** during the transition [36] — a deliberate resilience choice no other operator made.
- **Tre:** own network, SA first-mover, best Consistent Quality — but the 5G coverage gap (2.98) is structural, not fixable without new spectrum [36].
- **Post-3G transition risk (now resolved):** PTS warned that some devices would lose 112 access after 2G/3G shutdowns and **required Tele2, Telenor and Tre to guarantee emergency access — via a domestic roaming solution** [36]. Net4Mobility shut down both 2G and 3G on 1 Dec 2025 [36].

## 4. The regulatory/defense layer (the part rarely surfaced)

- **NIS2 has become Swedish law** (prop. 2025/26:28, July 2026) — stricter incident-prevention, risk-management and reporting duties for telecom as critical infrastructure; PTS runs active supervisory checks on spectrum-security conditions (including vendor-security requirements effective Jan 2025) [36].
- **Försvarsmakten's own submission to MSB** flags reserve power in core and mobile networks as *high-priority* — i.e., the known weak point in crisis scenarios is electricity, not operator competence; PTS has piloted mobile-site generator backup (Gotland) with results feeding mainland rollout.
- All four networks sit under the same critical-infrastructure regime — there is no "less regulated" operator among them.

## 5. Verdict — stability and incidents, deep-research edition

| Question | Answer with evidence |
|---|---|
| **Who has the most *incidents*?** | No public registry exists; all three hosts are critical infrastructure under NIS2/CER-grade rules. No recent major national outages found for any of them. Differences in *outage frequency* are not measurably significant. |
| **Who is most *reliable* as experienced?** | **Tre and Telenor statistically tied (943/944), Telia close behind (927)** [36] — Tre's reliability is excellent *within* its footprint. |
| **Where does Tre lose?** | Footprint, not stability: Coverage 6.55 vs Telia's 7.67; 5G coverage 2.98 vs 4.92 [36] — permanent dead zones, not incidents. |
| **Who has the most crisis-resilient architecture?** | Telia (2G to 2027 for emergencies, own everything, best populated-area coverage 7.67) and Net4Mobility (5G network-wide with explicit resilience focus, 99.9%) [9][36]; Tre strongest in cities, weakest footprint. |
| **Your household split (Fello/Telia + Vimla/Net4Mobility)?** | Validated by the data: the two hosts with the **top coverage scores and two different failure geometries** (isolated Telia grid vs shared Net4Mobility grid), both with 99%+ measured availability — and 112 now backed by a regulated domestic-roaming fallback after the legacy shutdown [36]. |

**The deep conclusion:** "stability" in Sweden isn't won by incident-avoidance — all three networks are engineered and regulated to near-parity there. The measurable differentiator is **Consistency × Coverage**: Tre maximizes consistency but minimizes footprint (your family's dead zones, now quantified as 2.98 on 5G coverage [36]); Telia maximizes footprint; Net4Mobility maximizes 5G coverage-per-population with a shared-grid blast radius. Your Fello+Vimla pairing sits on the two highest-coverage, highest-satisfaction, independently-failing networks — which is exactly what the crisis analysis recommended, now backed by measured reliability data rather than marketing.
